chapter_summary:
The Raspberry Pi's GPIO pins are digital. They can only be HIGH or LOW. However, many real-world effects need variable output, such as dimming an LED or controlling motor speed. PWM solves this by turning the pin on and off very quickly. The duty cycle, or the percentage of time the pin is on, determines the average power delivered to the load.

When an LED is driven by PWM at 50% duty cycle, it receives full power half the time and no power half the time. Because the switching happens faster than the human eye can perceive, the LED appears half as bright. Similarly, a motor receiving PWM at 75% duty cycle runs at about three-quarters of full speed.

In `gpiozero`, the `PWMLED` class makes fading easy:

```python
from gpiozero import PWMLED
from time import sleep

led = PWMLED(17)

while True:
    led.value = 0.0
    sleep(0.5)
    led.value = 0.5
    sleep(0.5)
    led.value = 1.0
    sleep(0.5)
```

The `value` property accepts a number between 0 and 1, where 0 is off and 1 is fully on. Values in between produce varying brightness.

To create a smooth fade effect, you can use a loop:

```python
from gpiozero import PWMLED
from time import sleep

led = PWMLED(17)

while True:
    for brightness in range(0, 101):
        led.value = brightness / 100
        sleep(0.02)
    for brightness in range(100, -1, -1):
        led.value = brightness / 100
        sleep(0.02)
```

Servo motors are controlled by PWM. A servo expects a pulse every 20 milliseconds. The width of the pulse determines the position. A 1.5 ms pulse typically centers the servo, 1.0 ms moves it to one extreme, and 2.0 ms moves it to the other. `gpiozero` provides a `Servo` class that handles this timing:

```python
from gpiozero import Servo
from time import sleep

servo = Servo(17)

servo.min()
sleep(1)
servo.mid()
sleep(1)
servo.max()
sleep(1)
servo.detach()
```

The Raspberry Pi has hardware PWM on GPIO 12, 13, 18, and 19. Hardware PWM is generated by dedicated circuitry and is very precise. Software PWM can be used on any GPIO pin but is created by the CPU and may be less stable under heavy load. For most beginner projects, `gpiozero` handles PWM transparently and you do not need to worry about the difference.

screens.title: PWM and Analog Output
screens.subtitle: How to simulate variable power from digital GPIO using Pulse Width Modulation

narration.text: In this chapter you'll learn how the Raspberry Pi creates the illusion of analog output using Pulse Width Modulation, or PWM. PWM rapidly switches a digital pin on and off; the fraction of time it stays on is the duty cycle and that percentage controls average power delivered to a device. You will see how LEDs dim smoothly with PWM, how motors and servos respond, and how gpiozero provides simple classes that handle timing and smoothing for us. We'll also look at which pins offer hardware PWM and why that matters for precision. A concrete example you will follow is building a fading LED on GPIO 17, then extending the idea to a two-LED opposite-fade activity. Finally, you'll compare hardware versus software PWM so you can pick the right pins for accuracy or convenience. By the end you will be able to explain duty cycle, use PWMLED to fade an LED, and move a servo to specific positions using pulse widths. Keep an eye out for a common misconception: PWM does not change voltage, it changes time at full voltage to control average power.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: PWM simulates varying output by changing the proportion of time a digital pin is HIGH. Duty cycle controls perceived power or position.

screens.title: What is PWM?
screens.subtitle: Definition, duty cycle, and why PWM simulates analog output

narration.text: Pulse Width Modulation is a technique that uses rapid on/off switching of a digital pin to control average power delivered to a device. Define duty cycle as the portion of each cycle when the pin is on, expressed as a percentage. Frequency is how many cycles occur per second. Together they determine the perceived output: for example, an LED receiving a fifty percent duty cycle spends half of each cycle on and half off, so it appears about half as bright. PWM does not change the supply voltage; instead it changes time at full voltage. A common misconception is thinking the voltage becomes intermediate; in reality the LED sees full voltage during on time and zero during off time. That timing, when fast enough relative to the device's response, yields a smooth perception. For motors, inertia averages the pulses into roughly proportional speed, while for servos we use pulse width in milliseconds to set angular position. Understanding PWM at this level helps you predict how different loads respond and choose suitable frequency and duty ranges for stable operation. Which device will you test first to feel the difference between duty and voltage?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: PWM controls average power by changing how long a pin is HIGH each cycle; duty cycle is the percentage of ON time.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › What is PWM?
Core Concept

Pulse Width Modulation

PWM switches a digital pin on and off rapidly. Duty cycle determines how much of each period is on, which sets average power.
Duty cycle
Percentage of time the signal is high during a cycle, e.g. 50% gives half power on average.
Frequency
How many on/off cycles per second; choose a frequency higher than the device's perception threshold.
Key Takeaway

PWM changes time at full voltage to vary average power; it does not change the voltage itself.

Concrete example
An LED at 50% duty cycle is on half the time and off half the time per cycle. Because switching is faster than the eye update rate, it looks half-bright.
Misconception
PWM changes time, not voltage. If you think the voltage drops, you'll misdiagnose dimming issues.
Pro tip
Use higher frequency for LEDs to avoid flicker; motors may respond differently due to inertia.
Check your understanding
If a PWM signal has a 25% duty cycle, what average power would the load receive? Answer: 25%.

narration.text: gpiozero provides a PWMLED helper that makes it easy to control brightness with a value between zero and one. The value property maps directly to duty cycle: zero means always off, one is always on, and intermediate values scale brightness. A short script that sets led. value to zero, point five, and one with pauses demonstrates the fundamental behavior and gives you confidence that the mapping is linear for perception. For smooth fades you typically loop from zero to one in small steps and sleep briefly between updates. When you run the fade loop on a real circuit with an LED and a current-limiting resistor, watch the transition speed and adjust the sleep interval for smoothness. screens.title: Creating a smooth LED fade
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step pattern: circuit, code, tune, observe

narration.text: A smooth LED fade requires four steps that you can practice and iterate on. Step one: build the circuit with an LED and appropriate resistor on the selected GPIO pin. Confirm polarity and avoid direct drives without a resistor. Step two: write a small script that uses PWMLED and a loop to vary the value. Start with large steps to verify behavior, then refine. Step three: tune timing and step size. Smaller increments and a sleep around twenty milliseconds produce smooth fades without visible stepping. Step four: observe and adjust for load and frequency. If the Pi is under significant C P U load and the fade stutters, consider using a hardware PWM pin or reduce background load. The process ends with a short test: try opposite fades on two LEDs so that when one is bright the other is dim. This helps solidify your intuition about how duty cycle proportions map to perceived power. When you're done, reflect on which step required the most tuning and why. Creating a smooth LED fade means assemble the circuit, code a loop, tune step size and delay, then observe and adjust for load.. In practical terms, step-by-step pattern: circuit, code, tune, observe. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Servo control with PWM
screens.subtitle: Pulse timing, typical pulse widths, and Servo helper methods

narration.text: Servos use PWM differently than LEDs. Instead of average duty controlling brightness, servos interpret the exact width of a pulse within a roughly twenty millisecond frame to set angle. Typical pulse widths are around one to two milliseconds: one millisecond moves to one extreme, about one and a half centers the servo, and two milliseconds moves to the other extreme. gpiozero's Servo class abstracts these details and offers methods such as min, mid, max and detach to move the servo safely. Using these helpers prevents you from handcrafting pulse timing and risking improper ranges. A concrete example is calling servo. min, waiting a second, then servo. mid and servo. max, observing the arm move between extremes. A misconception beginners have is to treat servo control like LED duty cycles; instead, focus on pulse width and the regular twenty millisecond repetition. If a servo jitters, it may be receiving irregular pulses or conflicting signals. Practice short sequences of min, mid, and max and listen for smooth movement; if movement is noisy, check wiring, power supply, and that pulses repeat consistently every twenty milliseconds.

keyIdea.title: Servo pulses
keyIdea.text: Servos use pulse width in milliseconds within a 20 ms frame to determine position; use gpiozero.Servo helpers for safe control.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Servo control with PWM
Definition

Pulse width controls position

Unlike LED brightness, servo position depends on the width of each pulse within a roughly twenty millisecond period. The width, measured in milliseconds, maps to physical angle.
Typical mapping
~1.0 ms → one extreme, ~1.5 ms → center, ~2.0 ms → opposite extreme.
gpiozero Servo
Use Servo class methods min, mid, max, and detach so you don't manage raw pulse timing yourself.
Concrete example
Call servo.min(), wait, servo.mid(), wait, servo.max(), and detach to observe centered and extreme positions. gpiozero handles the timing for you.
Common mistake
Treating servo control like LED duty. Remember to think in pulse width milliseconds rather than average duty percentage for position.
Key Takeaway

Servo position depends on pulse width; use gpiozero Servo helpers to avoid manual timing errors.

screens.title: Hardware PWM vs Software PWM
screens.subtitle: Understand precision, stability, and when to choose each

narration.text: There are two ways to generate PWM signals on a Raspberry Pi: hardware PWM and software PWM. Hardware PWM comes from dedicated circuitry on specific pins—GPIO 12, 13, 18, and 19—and produces very stable, precise waveforms regardless of C P U load. Software PWM can run on any GPIO pin because it uses C P U timing to toggle the pin, but its timing can vary if the processor is busy, causing jitter. For most beginner LED fades software PWM is perfectly adequate and gpiozero handles it transparently. However, if you need precise motor control, stable servo timing, or you run heavy background tasks, hardware PWM reduces timing errors. A common misconception is that software PWM always fails; in reality it is useful and flexible but less deterministic. The comparison on screen lists trade-offs: precision and stability favor hardware; flexibility and availability favor software. A simple test is to run a complex C P U task while observing the output; increased jitter indicates software PWM limitations. Which approach suits your project depends on how tolerant your device is to timing variations.

keyIdea.title: Choose by need
keyIdea.text: Hardware PWM is precise and stable on GPIO 12, 13, 18, 19; software PWM is flexible and can be used on any pin but may jitter under load.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Hardware PWM vs Software PWM
Comparison

Hardware vs Software

Hardware PWM
Generated by dedicated circuitry on specific pins. Offers precise timing even when the CPU is busy.
Software PWM
Uses CPU to toggle pins and can be used on any GPIO pin. Timing may vary under load.
When to choose
Hardware for precision devices; software for simple LEDs and flexible pin choices.
Quick test
Run a CPU-heavy task while observing PWM. If output jitters, prefer hardware PWM.
Hardware PWM pins
GPIO 12, 13, 18, 19
Remember these four pins when you need steady, low-jitter signals for motors or precision servo control.
Misconception check
Software PWM isn't broken; it simply depends on the CPU. For many beginner projects it works fine and gpiozero hides the details.
Pro tip

Start with software PWM. If you see timing instability, move the signal to a hardware PWM pin.

screens.title: Hardware PWM pins on the Raspberry Pi
screens.subtitle: Which pins support hardware PWM and practical notes

narration.text: The Raspberry Pi exposes hardware PWM on specific GPIO pins that have dedicated timing hardware. The pins listed in the chapter are GPIO twelve, thirteen, eighteen and nineteen. These pins can generate hardware-driven PWM signals that remain stable even if the C P U is busy with other tasks. This stability matters for precision servo movement or situations where jitter causes mechanical issues. For everyday LED fades, software PWM is often sufficient and more flexible because it works on any GPIO pin. A good practical rule is to prototype with software PWM on convenient pins; if you notice timing problems during load or you require precise motor control, move the signal to one of the hardware PWM pins. When wiring hardware PWM signals, ensure your power and ground references are solid and avoid sharing noisy supplies with motors. Keep in mind gpiozero will use hardware PWM where available, but knowing which pins are hardware-capable helps you plan projects that need reliability. Hardware PWM pins
The Raspberry Pi provides hardware PWM on four GPIO pins. Use these for stable, low-jitter signals.
GPIO 12
Hardware PWM channel available for precise timing.
GPIO 13
Paired hardware PWM pin for alternate channels.
GPIO 18
Common choice for PWM peripherals; stable under load.
GPIO 19
Another hardware PWM option; remember the set of four.
Practical notes
Start on any pin with software PWM. If timing becomes unstable under load or you need precise servo timing, move to a hardware PWM pin.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Build: fading two LEDs in opposite directions
Circuit steps
Wire LED with resistor to GPIO 17, and a second LED with resistor to GPIO 27. Share a common ground. Verify polarity and resistor values before powering.
Code pattern
from gpiozero import PWMLED
from time import sleep

led1 = PWMLED(17)
led2 = PWMLED(27)

while True:
    for i in range(0, 101):
        v = i / 100
        led1.value = v
        led2.value = 1 - v
        sleep(0.02)
Observation and tuning
If you see stepping, reduce step size or change delay. If one LED jitters under CPU load, try moving it to a hardware PWM pin for comparison.
Key Takeaway

Opposite fades illustrate how duty cycle proportions combine. Inverting values produces a smooth crossfade when tuned correctly.

screens.title: Common mistakes and troubleshooting
screens.subtitle: Resistors, step size, CPU load, and servo jitter

narration.text: Beginners often encounter predictable issues when working with PWM. First, omitting a current-limiting resistor on an LED can damage the LED or the Pi's GPIO pin. Always include the resistor and test with low duty cycles initially. Second, choosing too-large step jumps in a fade loop creates visible stepping rather than a smooth transition; reduce step increments or increase update frequency to fix it. Third, software PWM can jitter under C P U load. If the Pi is busy with other processes and output becomes unstable, move time-critical signals to hardware PWM pins or reduce background load. Fourth, servos can jitter when pulse widths are inconsistent or power is insufficient. Ensure a stable power source and consistent twenty millisecond repetition. If the servo still jitters, check wiring and try hardware PWM. When troubleshooting, isolate variables: test single LEDs first, then add complexity. These checks will save time and protect your components. After fixing issues, reflect on which change produced the most improvement and why. Common mistakes and troubleshooting means use resistors, refine step size, watch for cpu-induced jitter, and ensure stable power for servos.. screens.title: Bringing it together
screens.subtitle: When PWM solves problems and where to be cautious

narration.text: PWM is a practical bridge between digital outputs and the analogue behavior devices often need. Use PWM for dimming LEDs, controlling motor speed, and positioning servos. Remember to think in duty cycle percent for average power, and pulse width in milliseconds for servo position. Start projects on any convenient GPIO pin using software PWM and gpiozero helpers; they usually work well. If your application needs stable timing, particularly for precise motor control or stable servo movement under system load, move signals to hardware PWM pins: GPIO twelve, thirteen, eighteen, and nineteen. Always include proper resistors for LEDs and verify power requirements for motors and servos, using external power supplies when necessary. Lastly, practice changes one variable at a time: step size, delay, pin selection, and power source. This approach helps you quickly identify the cause of visual stepping or jitter.
